as not only to alarm but terrify the Postmaster

Yesterdays thunder storm, with its copi.
GUS rainfall of 227 inches, was one of the
series predicted for the present week in
Tuesdays HERALD. The drizzling rain that
prevailed during the day was due to the in
fluence of the cool northerly wind on the
heated and moisture-laden atmosphere, q
condensation of the vapor into rain being
produced. Such storms, although they may
cause temporary Inconvenience to great
many business people, are blessings for
which we cannot be too thankful at the
present season. While the city streets are
in many places reeking with filth and the
sewers charged with refuse matter in solid
forms, great drenching, cleansing rain
storm is sorely needed to preserve the health
of the city. Not only are the street cutters,
pavements and sewers washed but the air
itself is purified by the heavy downfall of
rain, the foul gases emanating from deposits
of garbage and other putrescent matter being
absorbed by the descending water. During
the passage of the area of high pressure
through Canada we will experience cloudy
weather, and fogs will prevail eastward
toward Newfoundland, rendering navigation
difficult From the westward we may expect
frequent thunder storms and recurring
periods of cloudiness and rain. Indeed, the
latter conditions will be likely to prevail
over the entire continent east of tho Rocky
Mountains in constantly and rapidly shift
ing areas. A tornado will probably occur in
the Mississippi and Ohio valleys during
to-day, the conditions being favorable for its
development. The rain belt has extended
from the Missouri to the Atlantic.

The adage that the Dutch have taken Hol-
land has rs venerable flavor as the famous
cheescs of the low country. For centuries the
Uollanders have been busy in reclaiming
their soil from the ocean. Nearly every por-
ton thus recovered had been dry land within
the historical period, and has sunk beneath
sea level since the date of the Roman civill-
zation. All other nations of the old world and
of the new trace back the title OF their lands
to rights born of conquest over their fel-
low-men. Holland alone has snatched
hers from the sea, regaining what had been
her OWL The work of resusctating the
drowned land is in general intimately asso-
ciated with the construction of canals. These
two objects are usually effected at once; in
many instances neither one would have been
practicable without the other. Especially has
This been the case with the newly constructed
ship-canal by which Amsterdam has just opened
a pathway to the sea. The pecuniary sue
cess of the project from the first depended
upon the value of the recovered land. The
engineering success resulted from system in
which drying the lands helped toward making
the canal.


The work now completed ranks among the
great engineering achievements Of the century.
In its kind it is second only to the Suez
Canal. A part of the machinery used on the
African isthmus was in fact transported to
Amsterdam, and did service in making the
North Sea Canal. Very greatly, indeed, was
Amsterdam in need of this direct communica-
ton with the ocean. The Zuyder Zee,
on a branch of which Amsterdam is sit
uated is scarcely navigable for vessels draw
ing more than five feet; it is bordered with
cities whose commerce has decayed. Amster-
dam would long since have followed the fate
of the other Zuyder Zee cities, except for the
North Holland Canal. That is a ship canal,
nominally u feet deep, 125 feet wide, and 81
miles long, which has hitherto been the sole
route for Amsteidam's ocean commerce. Prac-

More than . hundred victims of the
Brooklyn tragedy were inferred in Green
wood Cemetery yesterday. Some Of them
had been recognized and were fol-
lowed to their long home by sor-
rowing friends, but the great majority
were unknown to any one who had viewed
their remains, and as the great funeral cor
tege passed through the dense throng Of
citizens there was scarcely a spectator who
could not justly tremble for fear that
friend of his own might be represented by
the unrecognizable contents Of some one Of
the coffins. The whole city seemed to go
into mourning; even those who had lost no
friends could not be insensible to the great
sorrow of those about them, and for once
the flags at half-mast, the draped buildings
and the bated voices expressed for the living
even more sorrow than for the dead The
services at the great grave, though simple,
we're far from being perfunctory. The SER
mon, while acknowledging the wisdom and
goodness of Providence, only echoed the
heart questionings Of the thousands who
wonder for what purpose the terrible calam-
ity was allowed to occur. Brooklyn never
before knew SO solemn day, and her cti-
zens may well pray to be forever delivered
from another like it.

Had the decision of the Supreme Court
declaring the Enforcement law unconsti-
tutional been rendered at an earlier period,
before the republican party lost control

would forthwith have passed new bill
avoiding the objections made against that
which is now adjudged void. The Court
fully admits that Congress may pass a
law for insuring the civil and politi-
cal equality of the negroes. If the
republican party had sooner known that
by attempting too much they had accom-
plished nothing it would have been in
their power to substitute appropriate
legislation for the unconstitutional law
which they enacted But this decision of
the Supreme Court, coming when It does,
not only annuls the Enforcement act, but
puts that provision of the constitution in
allegiance which authorizes Congress to pass
laws for the protection of negro equality
After the INSCRIPTIONS abuses of leg
islation practised by the republican
party under color of that authority, and
which the Supreme Court has condemned,
the democrats are not likely to consent to
any further legislation on the subject. The
negroes, for the ensuing two years at least
will have to depend for protection on the
State governments. There will be no further
interposition of federal authority supported
by federal bayonets to support their rights
or redress their wrongs. This important
decision marks the beginning of a new era
in the political relations of the negro race in
our Southern States.


If the Southern governments should be
Just, humane and considerate, they can easily
detach their colored citizens from the repub-
lican party and virtually annihilate that
party throughout the South. The negroes
ment law with the broken Freedmen's Saw

ment that their rights have been no safer
than their money in the custody of the re-
publican party. Finding their hopes disap-
pointed, their confidence abused, and that
they must, after all, depend for protection and
prosperity on the communities with which
their lot is cast, they will be disposed to CO.
operate more cordially with their immediate
fellow citizens than they have ever been
since their emancipation. They have nothing
to depend upon now but their own industry
and sobriety and the justice and good will

Forty years ago to-day the morning
sun shown upon day than which that
Of Austerlltz or Bannockborn was not
more radiantly beautiful. Upon the HIS
torlc banks OF Buffalo Bayou stood 1888
Texans, under the leadership Of Hous-
ton and Rusk, confronting over 800
troops, the flower OF the Mexican
army, commanded by two OF their
ablest leaders, Santa Anna and Cos.
The flag OF the Lone Star State was
kissed by the soft gulf breezes az II
waved oyer the noblest and bravest
hearts, that ever throbbed In the breasts
OF men, while with insolent menace,
amid waving plumes and flashing Ian
ces, the Mexican officers unfurled to
the breeze their silken standard, over
legions Of hitherto victorious troops.
At half past three O'clock the Texan
artillery, which had been bravely
pushed forward TO within two hundred
yards OF the enemy's broastworks,
opened fire with canister and grape,
while the whole line advanced with
the terrible cry Of "Romember The Ata-
mol Remember La BohiaN


1t was brief, gallant, fierce, almost
meroless fight. In eighteen minutes,
the irresistible aud impetuous valor
OF the Texans had carried the day and
annlhilated the proud army OF Santa
Anna, the Napoleon OF the West. Six
hundred and thirty Mexicans bit the
dust, among them one General officer
two Lieutenant Colonies, five Cap
tains, and twelve Lieutenants. Two
hundred and eight were wounded, and
seven hundred and thirty prlponers
were captured, including President
General Santa Anna, General Cos, and
Colonel Almonte. One half of the Mex
lean army perished under the deadly
and unerrlng aim Of the Texan rifle
men.


The desperate struggle upon the
blood-stained field of San Jacinto was
one of the most decisive battles of the
world. 1t was a field which lights the
historic page with blaze Of glory. 1T
Is worthy Of all honor, and every
Texans heart should to-day beat re-
sponsive to the echo of San Jacinto's
guns.

The most extraordinary balloon adventure
on record has just happened to the aronauts
of the Alexandra Palace Company, London.
Having attained height of eight Thousand
feet, they three times crossed the Thames,
and descended in large meadow near Elt-
ham, Kent. They were just letting off the
gas when large bull charged them, below
ing furiously. They threw the two last bags
of sand out of the car, and barely escaped
through the rising of the balloon. The bull
scattered the sand bags over the ground,
and his horns, becoming entangled with the
grapnel iron, set the grapnel free, throwing
the aronaut out of the car through the jerk.
Fortunately, he succeeded in clutching the
netting, and, with his companions assis-
tance, was hauled into the car before It had
ascended many hundred feet. They then
sailed away for mile, and descended in
another meadow.

text:
We entered the large and spacious
hall chosen by Professor George for his
masquerade ut an early hour last
evening.


Brilliantly lighted and festooned
with sedar in the most graceful man
ner, with the wide sweeping walls
adorned with tiers of paintings, the
hall presented to the eye of the be-
holder rare and beautiful sight. In
the exquisite taste evinced by Profess
or George in these handsome decora-
tons we cannot speak too highly.


1t must have been near ten o'clock
when the hall began to fill rapidly
with the maskers. The sight was n
rare and beautiful one. There were
lovely girls adorned in the most varied
costumes that the taste Of mother or
sister could select,sparkling and bright,
sombre and grey, at times fitting past
like some dark dream, at other
moments some royal beauty
would sweep proudly on with
her jewelled dress flashing back
the radent rays of light which shone
upon her. Queens and princesses,
night and day, were there, and even
the PRESS was represented by the
fairest Of the fair. Brave knights and
gallant sailors were on every side; also
Boss Tweed, with his immense dla-
mond flashing back from his peniten-
tiary stripes, graced the occasion with
his portly presence; Rip Van Wrinkle,
grey and long-haired, and ALTERING Of
step after twenty long years of sleep,
was there; gorillas and! orangoutangs,
yankees and Indians, the tiger, the
horse, the cow--even the veritable
old devil himself kindly condeseend-
ed to put in an appearance.


Varied and picturesque beyond de-
scription was the scene when the dance
began, and amid its mazes the maskers
moved to and fro, to the stirring music
of the band.


Radient beauties danced with horrid
gorrillas, fair daughters of the white
race rested gracefully upon the arms of
some fierce savage, while some gentle
little beauty supported the hesitating
steps of Rip Van Winkle-kind, genial
old Rip. The COW scraped acquaint-
ance with the tiger, the orang-outang
with the horse, while yankees and
Irishmen were hail fellows well met
with the devil.


The occasion was pleasant one
long to be remembered, and it would
be supererogation to say that Prof
George made perfect success. We
left at late hour, everything then
going on as merry as marriage bell.

That stupidity illogical thing which we
call an Indian policy received q quaint
touch in despatch we printed yesterday
anent the way the red men regard the treat
ment the returning hostiles received at Fort
Peck. Mr.. Long Dog, it seems, who was
fresh from the hostile camp, claimed and re-
ceived first rate treatment at Fort Peck in
deed, it was with some difficulty Long Dog
was restrained from getting into bed with
the Indian agent himself. The effect of this
hospitality to a red-handed murderer upon
the peaceable agency Indians was notice.
able They complained that "when the
hostiles come in the agent shakes hands
with them and .fetes them, and it makes
them feel sorry they were not hostile, be-
cause then they would be treated much bet
ter" This is very natural. The agency
Indians have been kept in a state bordering
on starvation, while the savages who come
back with white scalps, Seventh cavalry
horses and all that the Indian admires un
der the name Of glory, are fed and coddled
and sent back with promises and presents
Now, the Indians know very well that Long
Dog and Lone Elk and Fast Dog, and oil
the other Elks and Dogs, are simply
spies, and we may rest assured that if
the winter passes without terrible
blow being given to the hostiles the
spring will open upon a campaign greater
in the numbers engaged and more bloody
and costly in result than the disastrous CAM
paign just closed. 1t is high time that the
government issued unmistakable orders to
the Indian agents respecting the way they
should receive all hostile Indians presenting
themselves. The picture of Long Dog furi-
ously demanding to sleep in the agents bed
at Fort Peck, while the peaceable Indians
without were regretting that they had not
been on the warpath, is highly suggestive of
the audacity of the victorious savages on one
hand and the imbecility Of our Ind iaL policy
on the other.

Five years ago peace was restored in France,

,European wars to which France is constantly
exposed that our Constitution is zone of the

MONTPELIER. VT, Jan. 4.-Ihe annual meeting OF
the Montpelier and Wells River Railroad Company
was held in the Village Hall here to-day. Five
loaded trains were required to bring the stockholders
and the hall was crowded to its utmost capacity.
No such excited public meeting has been held here
since the war Of 1912. The grand contest was Tor
the control of 1000 shares Of stock, held
by the town of Montpelier, the sale OF which had
been made few years ago by vote OF the town 10
J. w. Brook of Montpelier, while another sale
was made under an attachment for debt 10
A. X. Sartwell of East Cambridge, Mass.
A scene Of great confusion took pace
and the crowd rushed upon the stage, and struggle
for the possession of the records occurred. Coats
were torn hair pulled windows broken, the
stage scenery and pictures pulled down, enYelop-
ing the combatants, the seats and benches were
broken and many personal encounters ensued.
Joel Foster, clerk of the meeting, was chased around
the room but finally escaped with the records. The
meeting finally adjourned amid the widest excite
ment and confusion. The Brock party aiterward
met and elected Directors.

Election Weather.


The science of politics in the United States
involves q close study of the various
idiosyncrasies of the population by which
have been discovered certain laws that
govern the results Of elections, no matter
how important or exciting the issues may be.
Parties being but the aggregations of in
dividuals whose temperaments give color
to their opinions, it is well established
fact that avocations and surroundings in
their reaction on temperament determine the
bias of the individuals that make up parties.
Hence we find that considerable Importance
is attached by the leaders to conditions
that are apparently foreign to those that
produce political differences. The weather
has frequently exercised powerful in
fuence. in determining tho results
of popular elections. It has grown
into popular belief that fair weather
is good for the republican party, and
that bad weather is favorable to the
democrats Why this should be it is
not difficult to understand, especially in the
case of the larger cities Of the East. The re-
publican ranks are largely recruited from
the wealthier classes of the community, the
men who live in comfortable houses and
wear good clothes. On the other hand the
laborers, the men who earn small wages and
work with their hands, form the bono and
sinew Of the democratic masses. But these
conditions do not prevail equally over the
Union. In the West the farming classes,
the hardy pioneers of civilization, frequently
form the republican strength, while the pro-
fessional men and those engaged in trade
form that of the democratic party. The
Southern proprietors and business men,
like the Western, are by tradition and
condition democratic, while their la
borers are in the opposition ranks. In
the East and North we are i'm
porters and manufacturers. In the West
and South production and expectation form
the bases of prosperity. The election to-
day will no doubt be similarly influenced
throughout the country by the state of the
weather, as have former elections, and with
o view to informing the readers of the
HERALD on such an interesting subject we
present the following series of weather
probabilities for the several States, which
are arranged in alphabetical order:--


Alabama, cool and clear. Arkansas, cold
and clear. California, temperate apd clear.
Colorado, cool and clear. Connecticut, warm
and cloudy, with rain. Delaware, warm and
cloudy, probably with rain. Florida, warm

and clear, or partly cloudy. Iowa. cold and

Nevada, cool and clear. New Hampshire

ing toward night. North Carolina, warm

Montgomery Queen seems to know

patrOniZe amusements on the Pacific

igable and never-tiring manager has

nent among the celebrities of Mr..

lie, the beautiful French female Sam.
son, who carries an immense brass

that Queen intends outdoing all previ-
Gus efforts in the direction of amusing
the public with new and the very best
sensational performances. Mr.. Queen
has acquired fine reputation in Cali
fornia for giving more than he promi-
ses to the people for their money, and
his shows are regarded by the people

essaries. The big street demonstra-
ton on Monday, April Sd. will show

orable dealing can accomplish.

their entertainments. The Emperor expressed him.
self as much pleased with the exercises He says
Omaha is city which has made

lie subsequently visited the Omaha Smelling
Works, where the imperial party were shown all the
various processes employed in reducing the ores,
and the operations OF the powerful machinery and
arrangements for rolling and working the metal

nation OF this specimen OF our Industrial enterprise

section will be able to cultivate their crops
this year. No plowing has yet beendone on
account of the high water and unless the
rivers fall within the banks before the First
of May the chances are that only partial
crop can be raised. For the past three
weeks the water has flooded all the low
lands adjacent to the river shores and for
ten days 1t has been higher here than
for many years. The situation at present
is anything but cheerful. The railroads
leading west to Little Rock have been
flooded for ten days, and the trains ceased
running On the road between Chiot and
Pine Bluffs, two hundred miles south, and
have also been stopped by high water for
two mouths. The road between Vicksburg
and Monroe, ninty miles west of Washta
has been caved in and disabled for about the
same period. The people get about from

The Storm Moving Eastward.
By Associated Press.


WASHINGTON, Sept. 19-The Weather
Bureau synopsis for the past twenty four
hours says:


The hurricane that was on Monday morn
ing central near Buffalo, has moved slowly
eastward, and is now over New England,
the central depression having steadily di-
minished, with di minishing winds and rain
fall. Northeast winds and light rain pre-
vail over Northern New England, the st.
Lawrence Valley and Canadian provinces.
Northwest winds and light rain in New
York and over lake Ontario, but with partly
cloudy and clearing weather in the South
Atlantic and Middle States. The pressure
has fallen in the Northwest and Southwest,
with southerly winds, high temperature,
and increasing cloudiness.


The rivers fell on Monday at Cincinnati
and Louisville, but rose at Augusta, Cairo,
Memphis. and Vicksburg, and especially at
Pittsburg, Harper's Ferry, and elsewhere in
the Middle States.

The Moon, sweet Empress OF the Night,
Sits on thezenith Of her throne
In silent majesty and light


And gorgeous empire, all her own;
Her jewelled courtiers disappear
In timid twinklings, Len again..
Like meteOrs from some distant sphere,
Through loOp-holes flash like diadems.
The Garth is brisht and beautiful, as when
Its mistress smiled on Eden's bowers,
And bathed in loveliness each glen
And cool retreat, with silver showers
And that once-happy, sinless pair,-
Which. arm-in arm those blest arcades
And green swards traversed everywhere,
From dewy morn to ey ening shades
Oh! at this weird-like, mystic hour
This sweet and shadeless Noon Of Night
When all mid-Summer's lavish power
Crowns earth with June's transcendent


light


When over all the livried scene,
Like some glad hearted, blue.eyed boy,
The laughing earth, in pearly sheen,
Sheds all night long her tears Of joy
Sweetheart, in heaven, come and wait,
With fearful eyes and throbbing heart,
Beside that narrow, silent gate,


Where Life and Love and did part
l kiss thy monumental stone--


kneel beside thy tlower'decked grave,
Crushed but resigned--in prayer-alone-
Then am valiant, strong and brave.
Sweet Peace, like Heaven sdescendingd dov {
Steals calmly DER my anguished soul,
And signals from yon world above
Seem now to call me to that goal
Each sigh becomes a triumph passed.
Each sound q holy melody
And every tear shed, glass


That soft and sweetly mirrors thee.
Sweet Spirit, robed in Heavens light,
By Seraphs tended bright and fair,
Send thy dear kindred on their flight
To guard, surround me, everywhere
For every sin and guilt of mire


And murmur, mustforgiven be,
And my poor heart be pure as thine,
Ere can mate again with thee.

The stranger taking a ride over Ell
ther of the railroads running out of
this city cannot but be impressed
with the prolific character of the soil
over which he passes. And another
fact will also impress him, which is
the large acreage of cultivated land
that meets his gaze on every side.
People at distance are accustomed to
think of Los Angeles valley as rich
body of soil only partially cultivated.
This is true in general sense. There
is broad area of soil in our valley
that has never felt the plow share.
But the number of acres now seeded
is largely in excess of any former
year, and the crop prospects are bet
ter than for the past eight or ten sea-
sons, Along the Anaheim road one
sees broad fields of barley, rye and
corn all growing finely. About Dow
ney the fields look unusually prolnis-
ing. The same gratifying sight pre-
sents itself along the roads leading to
Orange and Santa Ana. San Jose
valley, from the San Gabriel river to
and beyond Spadra, never looked so
we'll as now. Down about Florence
and around Compton the farmers have
seeded largely and their fields promise
an abundant harvest. Everywhere
the prospect for large yield is very
encouraging, and everywhere the
farmers are happy and content. The
soil products of Los Angeles valley
this year will perhaps double those of
any former season.

lish them. The hero of the event had

lover, drove to Atchison, and thence 10

legally married according to the laws

loss early Saturday morning, ana a
very few inquiries satisfied him as 10
the cause of this coup detdt.. Whiie
the old gentleman raved anu sworei
he did not follow them. When they
returned was sufficient time for nm 10
get his revenge, and he bided MS
time with all the patience possible
Sure enough, the truant pair drove up

met them at the door, and demanded
his daughter, and the indomita6le
lover and new-made husband ln-
fromed him that he couldn't have her'

like u pirate, and threatened to take

Providentially the percussian cap was

who had been attracted by the
screams Of the young girl, appeared
ard drove the new husband away.


The father has now commenced suit
to recover his daughter, alleging that
she was under sixteen, and the point
remains to be decided.
